```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, error = FALSE)
options(width = 100)
```

This vignette covers fitting `terradish` models on large rasters, with
hundreds of thousands to millions of grid cells. It assumes you can already
fit and read a small model as shown in
[`vignette("v01-getting-started", package = "terradish")`](v01-getting-started.html).

The examples use the Ohio pond data from the other guides
(`vignette("v12-data-generation", package = "terradish")` describes how they
were made). That graph is small, so every example runs in seconds and the
guide can show real output. It teaches configuration and how to read each
diagnostic, not speed: the timings printed here say nothing about a large
raster. Time and memory depend on graph geometry, conductance contrast,
focal-site count, and hardware, so measure them on your own design.

**Goal.** Start with solver choice and domain sensitivity. Read the optional
sections on parallel workers, nuisance optimization, and curvature when a
measured computational problem calls for them.

```{r load}
library(terradish)
data(ohio_ponds)
coords <- ohio_ponds$ponds[c("x", "y")]

# Pond-level allele counts and the covariance response used in every guide.
g <- factor(ohio_ponds$samples$pond, levels = ohio_ponds$ponds$pond)
Y <- rowsum(ohio_ponds$snp, g, reorder = FALSE)
Y <- Y[ohio_ponds$ponds$pond, , drop = FALSE]
N <- 2 * as.numeric(table(g))
stopifnot(all(N == N[1]))
S <- cov_from_biallelic(Y, N) / N[1]

# Standardize once on the full domain, then build the graph.
covariates <- scale_covariates(terra::unwrap(ohio_ponds$forest500))
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords, directions = 8)
c(graph_vertices = nrow(surface$x), focal_sites = length(surface$demes))
```

The graph covers the full landscape, but the response is covariance among 24
ponds, so more raster cells add no sampled populations or marker information.
The fits below use the `nu = 40` working assumption from Getting Started.

```{r domain-map, fig.cap = "The full forest-context grid and sampled ponds. Computational shortcuts must preserve the routes needed for the biological question."}
terra::plot(covariates, main = "Standardized 500 m forest context")
points(coords, pch = 21, bg = "white", cex = 0.7)
```

**How to read the map.** The ponds are spread across most of the raster, and
paths connecting them can run through any part of it. A tightly cropped map
is therefore not automatically an equivalent, faster analysis (see the
cropping section below).

## When a landscape is "large"

`terradish` builds a weighted graph over the raster grid and solves linear
systems on it to get resistance distances among focal sites. The cost grows
with the number of graph vertices (the raster cells that are not missing).
Two stages matter, and they have different limits:

1. **Graph construction.** `conductance_surface()` always performs one
   sparse Cholesky factorization of the graph and stores it in the returned
   object, whatever `solver` you request later. Construction memory
   therefore sets the first limit: a raster too large for that one
   factorization cannot produce a graph.
2. **Fitting.** Every likelihood, gradient, and Hessian evaluation solves
   the system again with updated conductances. The `solver` argument acts
   here, where repeated solves dominate the run time.

The **inference** machinery (standard errors and confidence intervals) keeps
its form at any size. Larger analyses can include more focal sites, and
Wishart precision still depends on the supplied effective degrees of freedom,
`nu` (see the information section below).

As a calibration, in one development test on a single machine, version 1.1.1
built the graph for a one-million-cell raster in under a minute and fitted
models on it in minutes to tens of minutes on one core. Read that as one
machine's result, not a guarantee. There is no universal cell-count limit,
because missing cells, graph connectivity, conductance contrast, and the
number of focal sites all change the cost.

---

## Choosing a solver

Both `terradish()` (the fitting wrapper) and `terradish_algorithm()` (one
likelihood and gradient evaluation) take a `solver` argument. The solver
changes **how** the resistance-distance system is solved during fitting, not
the statistical model. Iterative solvers should agree with the direct solver
within numerical tolerance, though not necessarily bit for bit.

```{r solver-calls}
# direct (the default): exact sparse Cholesky solves
direct_seconds <- system.time(
  fit <- terradish(S ~ forest500, surface,
                   measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40,
                   solver = "direct")
)[["elapsed"]]

# amg: algebraic multigrid, an iterative solver for very large graphs
amg_seconds <- system.time(
  fit_amg <- terradish(S ~ forest500, surface,
                       measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40,
                       solver = "amg")
)[["elapsed"]]

# The two solvers must agree on the estimate and the log-likelihood.
rbind(direct = c(forest500 = coef(fit)[["forest500"]],
                 logLik = as.numeric(logLik(fit)), seconds = direct_seconds),
      amg    = c(forest500 = coef(fit_amg)[["forest500"]],
                 logLik = as.numeric(logLik(fit_amg)), seconds = amg_seconds))
```

**How to read the output.** The coefficient and log-likelihood agree to
within `r signif(max(abs(coef(fit) - coef(fit_amg)), 1e-12), 1)` and
`r signif(max(abs(as.numeric(logLik(fit)) - as.numeric(logLik(fit_amg))), 1e-12), 1)`,
which is the check to repeat on a manageable case before you trust an
iterative solver on a large one. On this small graph `amg` took
`r round(amg_seconds, 1)` seconds against `r round(direct_seconds, 1)` for
`direct`, because multigrid setup costs more than a small factorization.
Its advantage appears only on very large graphs.

The choices are:

- **`direct`** (default) uses sparse Cholesky factorization. The factor can
  hold many more nonzero entries than the graph, so its memory can grow
  rapidly.
- **`amg`** uses algebraic multigrid, an iterative solver that avoids
  repeated factorization during fitting. It does not remove the
  factorization that `conductance_surface()` performs, so it does not lower
  the memory needed to build the graph. Its convergence depends on
  conductance contrast and graph structure, and strong barriers can require
  more iterations or tighter solver settings.
- **`auto`**, with default controls, uses `direct` below 1,500,000 graph
  vertices and `amg` at or above. The number of focal sites does not override
  this switch, and `solver_control$auto_amg_min_vertices` changes the threshold.

Before a long fit, `terradish_assess_settings()` runs short optimizer and
solver probes on your graph and recommends settings, and
`terradish_solver_benchmark()` times each direct factorization:

```{r assess-settings}
settings <- terradish_assess_settings(S ~ forest500, surface,
  measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40)
settings                        # graph size, probe timings, and a verdict
settings$recommended$solver     # pass to terradish(solver = ...)
settings$recommended$optimizer  # pass to terradish(optimizer = ...)
```

**How to read the assessment.** The first lines report graph size (also in
`settings$profile`). `Recommended settings` names the fastest probe that
reached an acceptable log-likelihood: here the `r settings$recommended$optimizer`
optimizer and the `r settings$recommended$solver` solver.
`settings$recommended` holds those settings as a plain list to pass to
`terradish()`. `Optimizer probes` lists each short run with its elapsed
seconds and the log-likelihood it reached after a few steps, so a faster
probe with a clearly lower `loglik` is not a better choice. The probes stop
early by design, and their log-likelihoods are not fitted optima.

On a graph this small every probe finishes in a fraction of a second, so
the ranking mostly reflects timer noise and can change between runs. The
recommendation can also name a solver backend that `?terradish` marks as
experimental. Run the assessment on your full raster, and treat it as a
speed probe: it does not show that a fit converges or that the measurement
model suits your data.

```{r solver-benchmark}
# Setup, solve, and total seconds for each direct factorization.
terradish_solver_benchmark(surface)
```

**How to read the benchmark.** Each row is one factorization. `setup_time`
is the factorization, `solve_time` is the solve for all focal sites, and
`total_time` is their sum. The smallest `total_time` names the
factorization to request with `solver_control = list(factorization = ...)`.
Times this close to zero do not separate the options, so repeat the
benchmark on your full raster before choosing.

Solver choice applies to every symmetric resistance model, whatever the
`conductance_model` (`loglinear_conductance`, `smooth_loglinear_conductance`,
the Gaussian scale-aware model) or measurement model (`mlpe`,
`leastsquares`, `generalized_wishart`, `wishart_covariance`).

After a fit, use the same diagnostics as for a small graph, starting with the
fitted-response scatter, and keep the fitted graph for conductance mapping.
The other guides show these plots, so the recipe is not run here.

```{r large-fit-plots, eval = FALSE}
plot(fit, type = "fit")  # observed versus fitted covariance for this response
library(ggplot2)
maps <- plot(fit, type = "surface", data = surface)
C <- conductance(surface, fit)
map_limits <- range(terra::values(C), na.rm = TRUE)

# Keep all cells and share limits across the estimate and both bounds.
for (p in maps) {
  print(p + scale_fill_viridis_c(
    trans = "log10", limits = map_limits,
    breaks = c(0.01, 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20),
    name = "Conductance\n(log color scale)"
  ))
}
```

Map colors run from dark purple (low conductance) to yellow (high). Equal
color steps are equal ratios, labels stay in conductance units, and the
estimate and bounds share limits without clipping.

A smooth map does not establish solver accuracy. Check that estimates and
likelihoods agree with a direct solve on a manageable case, and inspect both
outer and nuisance convergence. Marginal-response plots need a graph solve at
every plotted value, so start with `n = 25` on a large graph.

---

## Information and effective degrees of freedom

For Wishart fits, `nu` is an effective degrees-of-freedom value that you
supply, not automatically the marker count.
Changing `nu` leaves the optimum unchanged in theory and scales interior
standard errors in proportion to `1 / sqrt(nu)`, which `terradish_rescale_nu()`
shows without refitting. See
[`vignette("v02-wishart-covariance", package = "terradish")`](v02-wishart-covariance.html)
for choosing `nu` and
[`vignette("v04-model-comparison", package = "terradish")`](v04-model-comparison.html)
for reporting inference across plausible values.

## Cropping and coarse warm starts

Cropping removes alternative routes outside the retained domain and can
increase resistance between sites even when every site stays inside the crop.
In an unpublished development check on one test landscape, cropping raised
resistance by 15 to 23% with a two-cell buffer and by 1 to 2% with a ten-cell
buffer. Values will differ on your landscape, so compare progressively wider
buffers with the same response, sites, formula, and covariate scaling.

```{r crop-sensitivity}
# Scale on the original domain once (done above), then crop. Buffers are in
# map units: 2, 10, 25, and 50 cells of this 100 m raster.
buffers <- c(2, 10, 25, 50) * max(terra::res(covariates))
buffer_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(buffers, function(buffer) {
  cropped_surface <- conductance_surface(
    covariates, coords, directions = 8, crop_buffer = buffer
  )
  cropped_fit <- terradish(S ~ forest500, cropped_surface,
                           measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40)
  interval <- confint(cropped_fit)
  data.frame(buffer_m = buffer, vertices = nrow(cropped_surface$x),
             forest500 = coef(cropped_fit)[["forest500"]],
             lower = interval[1, 1], upper = interval[1, 2])
}))
print(buffer_table, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)

# The uncropped fit, and the package's rule of thumb for a small buffer.
c(full_graph = coef(fit)[["forest500"]],
  half_max_site_distance_m = max(dist(coords)) / 2)

# crop_to_focal_buffer() crops the raster stack directly, if you prefer to
# build the graph yourself; it keeps the scale_covariates() metadata.
cropped <- crop_to_focal_buffer(covariates, coords, buffer = 200)
c(full = terra::ncell(covariates), cropped = terra::ncell(cropped))
```

**How to read the output.** Compare estimates and intervals across buffers.
With a `r buffer_table$buffer_m[1]` m buffer the graph keeps
`r buffer_table$vertices[1]` of `r nrow(surface$x)` vertices and the forest
coefficient is `r round(buffer_table$forest500[1], 2)`, against
`r round(coef(fit)[["forest500"]], 2)` on the full graph. At
`r buffer_table$buffer_m[2]` m it is `r round(buffer_table$forest500[2], 2)`,
and from `r buffer_table$buffer_m[3]` m the crop retains the whole raster and
reproduces the full fit. The tight crops change the estimate because they
remove routes, not because they add information. If the coefficient or its
interval keeps changing as the buffer widens, keep widening until it
stabilizes. `terradish_distance()` compares the fitted resistance distances
directly.

Both cropping routes print a message (hidden in this guide's output) when
the buffer is less than half the largest distance between sites, which is
`r round(max(dist(coords)) / 2)` m here, so the first three buffers trigger
it. Treat the message as a prompt to run this check, not as proof that a
larger buffer is adequate.

Coarse rasters can provide starting values, but coarsening changes both routes
and covariate summaries, so the supported workflow requires exact refinement
on the original graph:

```{r coarse-warm-start}
# Fit on a raster aggregated by 4, then by 2, then refine on the full graph.
fit_coarse <- terradish(
  S ~ forest500, surface,
  measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40,
  approximation = "coarse_raster",
  approximation_control = list(factor = c(4, 2), exact_refine = TRUE)
)
c(exact = coef(fit)[["forest500"]], coarse_start = coef(fit_coarse)[["forest500"]],
  outer_code = fit_coarse$convergence$code,
  nuisance_code = fit_coarse$fit$subproblem$convergence)
```

**How to read the output.** After exact refinement the warm-started fit
matches the direct fit, and both convergence codes are 0. Inspect
convergence after the final refinement, because a converged coarse fit does
not establish convergence on the original graph. `terradish_grid()` accepts
only `approximation = "none"`, and coarse-only likelihoods are not supported
for ranking models.

---

## Storing large fitted objects

Fitted conductance and measurement-model closures can retain their
construction environments, including large graph objects. That helps
prediction but can make `saveRDS()` files much larger than the coefficient
table suggests. Use `slim_terradish()` when the saved object is for inference
summaries rather than later prediction:

```{r slim-fit}
# fit is the unslimmed model fitted above.
fit_slim <- slim_terradish(fit)
fit_slim$storage

saveRDS(fit_slim, file.path(tempdir(), "terradish-fit-slim.rds"))
```

**How to read the output.** `dropped` lists the removed components, and
`bytes_before` and `bytes_after` give the in-memory size of the fit before
and after slimming. Passing `slim = TRUE` to `terradish()` does the same at
fit time.

The default removes `submodels` and `leverage`. Coefficients, likelihood,
Hessian-based summaries, fitted values, diagnostics, and permutation
simulation remain available. Conductance prediction and most plot types do not,
because they must reevaluate the removed closures. Slimming is irreversible, so
keep the formula, graph, response, and an unslimmed fit whenever you may need
prediction or model reconstruction. Add `"response"` to `drop` only when the
response must be excluded from the archive, because that also removes the
strongest stored check for later model comparison.

---

## Optional tuning: workers, nuisance optimization, and curvature

Read these subsections only when a measured computational problem calls for
them.

### Parallel workers

Parallel execution is **experimental**. `cores > 1` requests PSOCK workers on
every operating system, for supported Hessian and partial-derivative
calculations and not for every step of a fit. On Windows, one worker pool is
kept for the whole fit instead of being rebuilt for each evaluation, and it is
stopped before return, so fitted objects hold no live workers. AMG and the
cached CHOLMOD backend ignore this setting. On small graphs, worker startup
and data transfer can make multiple cores slower than one, so benchmark
`cores = 1` first and compare elapsed time and results with the requested
worker count.

Use one level of parallelism at a time. Fixed-domain cross-validation, for
example, evaluates folds serially and passes `cores` to each fit.

### Controlling the nuisance profile

Each trial of the conductance parameters profiles the measurement model's
nuisance parameters. Smooth conductance models paired with
`generalized_wishart` can make this two-level optimization costly, because
each outer step may need many inner Newton steps. This recipe therefore
switches from the covariance response `S` to its squared-distance form `D`
and to `generalized_wishart`, the pairing where the cost arises. The inner
optimizer already warm-starts from the previous nuisance solution. Use
`measurement_control` to inspect or tune it separately from `control`:

```{r measurement-control, eval = FALSE}
D <- dist_from_cov(S)  # coherent squared distances from the pond covariance
fit_smooth_gw <- terradish(
  D ~ s(forest500, df = 3),
  surface,
  conductance_model = smooth_loglinear_conductance,
  measurement_model = generalized_wishart,
  nu = 40,
  optimizer = "bfgs",
  control = NewtonRaphsonControl(maxit = 80, verbose = TRUE),
  measurement_control = NewtonRaphsonControl(
    maxit = 40,
    ctol = 1e-8,
    ftol = 1e-10,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)

fit_smooth_gw$fit$subproblem
```

The returned `convergence` code and `iters` count describe the final nuisance
profile. A code of 0 means convergence, 1 means the profile reached `maxit`,
and 2 means a line-search failure. Do not loosen tolerances just to remove a
warning. First inspect coefficient stability, gradient size, the likelihood,
and sensitivity to tighter settings, because overly loose profiling can change
the fitted likelihood surface.

### Curvature for standard errors

`terradish()` and `terradish_algorithm()` take `curvature = c("exact",
"gauss_newton")`. Both options share the objective and gradient and differ
only in the Hessian used for optimization and standard errors.

```{r curvature-calls}
# exact (default): full observed Hessian. This is `fit` from above.
# gauss_newton: information-based curvature, same model and response.
fit_gn <- terradish(S ~ forest500, surface,
                    measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40,
                    curvature = "gauss_newton")
rbind(exact        = c(estimate = coef(fit)[["forest500"]],
                       std_error = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[[1]]),
      gauss_newton = c(estimate = coef(fit_gn)[["forest500"]],
                       std_error = sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_gn)))[[1]]))
```

**How to read the output.** The two fits reach the same estimate, because
they share the objective. Their standard errors differ:
`r round(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[[1]], 3)` with the exact Hessian and
`r round(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_gn)))[[1]], 3)` with Gauss-Newton curvature, a
ratio of `r round(sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_gn)))[[1]] / sqrt(diag(vcov(fit)))[[1]], 2)`.
A gap of this size means the omitted terms are not negligible for this fit,
so report which curvature produced an interval.

- **`exact`** uses the full observed Hessian.
- **`gauss_newton`** drops the two residual-weighted second-derivative terms,
  leaving the **Gauss-Newton information** curvature. It needs only first
  derivatives of conductance and is positive semidefinite when the retained
  measurement-model curvature is. It flows unchanged into `vcov()`,
  `summary()`, and `confint()`, so standard errors become asymptotic,
  information-based errors. It approaches the exact Hessian when the omitted
  terms are negligible, not merely because a fit has converged.

**How to choose.** Use the `exact` default for routine work. Reach for
`gauss_newton` when the optimizer struggles with an indefinite Hessian far
from the optimum, or when you want strictly information-based standard
errors. The package tests check `gauss_newton` for `leastsquares` and
`wishart_covariance`, and the shipped benchmark exercises it with
`generalized_wishart`.

For `mlpe` the two curvatures can disagree. A package test evaluates both
at the same optimum on the `melip` data. The coefficients agree, but the
Gauss-Newton standard errors differed from the exact ones by 3% to 14% in
three configurations and by about a factor of two in a fourth, with no
consistent direction. Report `exact` standard errors for `mlpe` fits, and
compare both options before relying on `gauss_newton` with any other
pairing.

The benchmark in `inst/benchmarks/benchmark-curvature-large-landscape.R`
reproduces this comparison at a chosen size. It simulates a
`generalized_wishart` squared-distance response from known conductance
parameters on a synthetic heterogeneous raster, then fits the same model with
each curvature option.

```{r curvature-benchmark-run, eval = FALSE}
source(system.file("benchmarks", "benchmark-curvature-large-landscape.R",
                   package = "terradish"))

bench <- run_curvature_large_landscape_benchmark(CONFIG)
bench$comparison
```

The default case (`side = 96`, `solver = "auto"`) is small enough to run
during review. For the large regime, copy `CONFIG` and increase `side`. The
default `auto` switches to AMG at 1,500,000 vertices, or set
`solver = "amg"` to force it at a smaller size.

**How to read the benchmark.** Compare coefficients and likelihoods first,
then standard errors, Hessian eigenvalues, and elapsed time, because matching
point estimates do not guarantee matching curvature. A large difference in
uncertainty warrants checking residuals, conditioning, and model
misspecification before choosing the faster option.

---

## Quick reference: computational settings

```{r quick-ref, eval = FALSE}
# 1. Build the graph once. This step performs one direct factorization.
surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords, directions = 8)

# 2. Probe settings on the full graph before a long fit.
settings <- terradish_assess_settings(S ~ forest500, surface,
  measurement_model = wishart_covariance, nu = 40)
terradish_solver_benchmark(surface)

# 3. Fit. "auto" keeps the direct solver below 1,500,000 vertices and
#    switches to AMG at or above; curvature stays at the exact default.
fit <- terradish(S ~ forest500, surface,
                 conductance_model = loglinear_conductance,
                 measurement_model = wishart_covariance,
                 nu = 40,
                 solver = "auto")
# Options for a measured problem, not defaults:
#   solver = "amg"              # force the iterative solver
#   curvature = "gauss_newton"  # information-based standard errors

summary(fit)                    # check the Convergence line first

# 4. If you crop, refit with wider buffers until the estimate stabilizes.
cropped_surface <- conductance_surface(covariates, coords, directions = 8,
                                       crop_buffer = 1000)

# 5. Optional archival copy when prediction from the saved object is unnecessary.
fit_archive <- slim_terradish(fit)
saveRDS(fit_archive, file.path(tempdir(), "fit-archive.rds"))
```

## Summary of key functions

| Function | Purpose |
|----------|---------|
| `conductance_surface()` | Build the weighted graph over the raster grid; `crop_buffer` crops it |
| `terradish()` | Fit the model; takes `solver` and `curvature` |
| `terradish_algorithm()` | One likelihood and gradient evaluation; same `solver` and `curvature` |
| `crop_to_focal_buffer()` | Crop with an explicit map-unit buffer; check domain sensitivity |
| `terradish_assess_settings()` | Compare computational settings on the current graph |
| `terradish_solver_benchmark()` | Time each direct factorization on the current graph |
| `slim_terradish()` | Remove prediction closures and other optional large components before storage |
